item.title: Jingisukan Guide: Hokkaido's Grilled Lamb BBQ & Where to Eat
item.description: Jingisukan (“Genghis Khan”) is Hokkaido’s beloved grilled-mutton barbecue, a smoky, sociable feast named for the dome-shaped grill said to resemble a warrior’s helmet. Diners cook lamb or mutton and a pile of vegetables — onions, beansprouts, cabbage, pumpkin — over the convex iron grill, where juices run down to flavour the veg around the rim. Washed down with ice-cold beer in a summer beer garden or a lively grill house, it’s one of Hokkaido’s most fun and convivial meals.

item.title: Sapporo Guide: Odori Park, Susukino & Things to Do
item.description: Sapporo, Hokkaido’s vibrant capital and Japan’s fifth-largest city, is the gateway to the north and a destination in its own right. Laid out on an easy American-style grid, it centres on the long green ribbon of Odori Park, runs north to the historic Clock Tower and former government buildings, and south into the neon buzz of Susukino, one of Japan’s great nightlife and dining districts. Add legendary food — miso ramen, soup curry, jingisukan and crab — plus year-round festivals, and Sapporo is the perfect base for exploring Hokkaido.

item.title: Sapporo Soup Curry Guide: What It Is & Where to Eat
item.description: Soup curry is a Sapporo original and one of Hokkaido’s most addictive dishes — a fragrant, spiced, brothy curry that’s worlds apart from the thick Japanese curry-rice found elsewhere. A light but deeply flavoured soup, often built on chicken or seafood stock and a blend of spices, comes brimming with big chunks of Hokkaido vegetables — pumpkin, lotus root, peppers, broccoli — and a hero protein like fall-off-the-bone chicken leg. You choose your spice level and eat it by dipping spoonfuls of rice into the soup.

item.title: Yosakoi Soran Festival Guide: Dates, Where to Watch & Access
item.description: Every June, Sapporo explodes with colour, music and motion for the Yosakoi Soran Festival — one of Japan’s most exhilarating dance events. Hundreds of teams, tens of thousands of dancers in bold costumes, surge through the streets and across stages, naruko clappers in hand, to powerful remixes of Hokkaido’s traditional “Soran Bushi” fishing song. Born only in 1992, the festival fuses Kochi’s yosakoi dance with Hokkaido’s sea-shanty heritage into a thrilling, modern spectacle that fills Odori Park and the city for several days.

item.title: Best Hotels & Ryokan in Hokkaido: Where to Stay in 2026
item.description: Hokkaido’s vast geography — 83,000 km², roughly the size of Austria — means accommodation strategy varies dramatically by destination. Sapporo offers urban hotel convenience; Niseko delivers world-class ski resort lodging; and the onsen towns of Noboribetsu and Jozankei provide some of Japan’s finest hot spring ryokan experiences. Best Areas to Stay in Hokkaido Sapporo — Best Hub for All Seasons Japan’s fifth-largest city. Excellent restaurants, the Sapporo Snow Festival in February, and train access to many Hokkaido highlights.

item.title: Hokkaido Festivals 2026: Sapporo Snow Festival, Yosakoi Soran & Lavender
item.description: Hokkaido’s festivals are as seasonal as its landscape — in winter, ice and snow; in spring, flowers; in summer, lavender and beer; in autumn, harvest and cranes. The key distinction from festivals elsewhere in Japan is scale: the Sapporo Snow Festival’s main sculptures are built by the Japan Self-Defence Forces using military engineering equipment, and the Yosakoi Soran festival deploys 30,000 dancers across a city. This guide covers the major events with specific advice on what most visitors miss and how to experience each festival beyond the standard tourist circuit.

item.title: Hokkaido Goshuin Guide: Hokkaido Shrine, Hakodate & Shiretoko Stamps
item.description: Hokkaido’s goshuin culture reflects the island’s young history — the shrines here were established in the Meiji era (post-1869), not centuries earlier, which means their architectural style is cleaner, their administrative records are complete, and their goshuin designs reflect a conscious aesthetics decision rather than an accumulated tradition. The stamp designs at Hokkaido’s major shrines often reference the specific natural feature of their location (crane imagery at Kushiro, the volcanic context at Noboribetsu) and the kaitaku (development) history that brought these institutions into existence.

item.title: Hokkaido Sightseeing: Sapporo, Hakodate, Otaru & Beyond
item.description: Hokkaido’s sightseeing does not fit the standard Japan template. The island was only formally incorporated into the Japanese state in 1869 — before that, it was Ainu territory supplemented by a small number of Matsumae Domain outposts. The colonial infrastructure (kaitaku, development) was built in the Meiji era with American agricultural advisors and a European city-planning sensibility that gives Sapporo its wide boulevards and Hakodate its Western hillside district. The result is a Japan that feels different at a structural level — more space, a younger built environment, and a relationship with the land that reflects 150 years of active settlement rather than 1,500 years of layered culture.

item.title: Best Ramen in Sapporo: A Local's Guide
item.description: Best Ramen in Sapporo: A Locals Guide to Hokkaido’s Soul-Warming Bowl If you’ve ever slurped a bowl of ramen in Tokyo or Osaka and thought, “This is as good as it gets,” I need you to reconsider. Because Sapporo — Hokkaido’s snow-dusted, food-obsessed capital — is where ramen transcends from a quick meal into something approaching a spiritual experience. This best ramen in Sapporo locals guide exists because, after living in Japan for 15 years and making more trips to Hokkaido than I can count, I’m convinced that Sapporo is the single greatest ramen city in the entire country.
